utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's Mr. Pantelic continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have only a few questions left for you. In connection with certain replies you gave to the Prosecutor. Tell me, Mr. Zaric: The Prosecutor asked you about the document which was actually the decision of the People's Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the strategic goals of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember -- [In English] Exhibit number --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, my friend. It's P5, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, please, Mr. Zaric: The framework of these goals was in fact more or less the territory of the present-day Republika Srpska; is this correct? If you can remember.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But this referred to the territorial component of the Serbian people as a subject?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's the conclusion that can be drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This territory, with greater or smaller differences, is the territory recognised in Dayton in this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina today; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, the Prosecutor asked you something in connection with your book, but in fact I have another question before I put this one. It is not contentious in this case, and you spoke of the fact that the previous territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, as of 1991, was divided in mid-April 1992 into the Serbian and Croatian part; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Right away. This became quite clear immediately after the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the part which practically became the Serbian municipality of Samac, the Serbian population was in the majority; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So it is not contentious that the same situation obtains today. The pre-war territory of the municipality of Samac has been divided and now there is Domaljevac Samac, belonging to the Federation, and the remainder belonging to the Republika Srpska, which is called the municipality of Samac; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And part of the pre-war municipality of Samac, from 1991, that's Prud, it belongs to Odzak; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to this line of questioning. Mr. Pantelic is permitted, I understand, to ask questions which have affected his client's interest arising from my cross-examination. I don't recall asking anything about demographics or population changes or municipal boundaries when I cross-examined Mr. Zaric. In my submission, it doesn't really arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, respectfully, this is Defence case. Our position is that there was a division of the pre-war territory of municipality of Samac. My learned friend asked Mr. Zaric whether the Serb -- Bosnian Serbs were in minority on the territory of municipality of Samac. And it was something which was unclear in the cross-examination. So I just want to clear it up, to see where, on which territory we are speaking, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. You can cross-examine. I remember that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And finally, Mr. Zaric, a few questions which my learned friend the Prosecutor put you in connection with some parts of your book, where you describe Dr. Simic, his political standpoint, and so on. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The SDS party is still active in Republika Srpska, that is, in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And a member of the SDS is at present also a member of the collective presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Paravac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The SDS was not in power during the previous term of office because party coalitions were set up along other lines; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were times when it was not in power at the level of Republika Srpska, but in certain municipalities it was in power.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As regards Samac, you're a member of the socialist party of the Republika Srpska. You have already told us that.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you personally, as a member of the SPRS, are practically a political opponent of the SDS. We are now talking about party platforms.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Platforms, and also ideological views. I am a political opponent of that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But we shall agree that the only judge of political platforms are election results?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That is the most democratic way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't have further questions for this witness. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, during your cross-examination, the Prosecutor asked you something about the detention of large numbers of Muslims and Croats during the war. So can you tell us: Were there any Croats or Muslims who were never detained during the war in the municipality of Bosanski Samac, where the Serbian authorities were in charge?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did members of the Muslim and Croatian people remain living in their homes in Samac throughout the war, in certain numbers?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A certain number of them remained living in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor asked you about the structure of the JNA, the military districts, the security administration, and other parts of the army, and you told him that the headquarters of the 17th Corps of the JNA was in Tuzla, that the commander was Savo Jankovic, a general, and that the headquarters of the 2nd Military District was in Sarajevo, and that at its head was General Milutin Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, when the attack on the army convoy of the JNA took place, which was withdrawing from the barracks where the command of the 2nd army district in Sarajevo was located?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but I know that this was sometime in May, I think, and this 2nd convoy from Tuzla, which was also attacked, I think this was on the 15th of May, 1992. I know that both convoys experienced attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. Are you aware of the fact that soldiers of the JNA, before that, were surrounded for days in the barracks of Husinska Buna in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object on two bases. One, Mr. Zaric is testifying, and I do ask that he be directed not to lead in his re-examination. And secondly, this has absolutely nothing to do with anything I asked in relation to the takeover before. The closest I got was I asked about JNA -- or depletion of the strength of the JNA in the 17th Corps before -- in 1991 and 1992, before the JNA withdrew. The only questions I asked in relation, that I can recall asking in relation to the JNA after the withdrawal were when Mr. Zaric went to Belgrade and his reasons for going to Belgrade, nothing about attacks in Tuzla on JNA convoys, which are a long way from the indictment material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. You've heard what Mr. Re has said, leading the witness; and then, secondly, the content, the material of your question, being outside the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understand the objection raised by the Prosecutor, and I understand your instructions. I cannot agree, however, that the Prosecutor, in his cross-examination, did not put questions in connection with the situation and the organisation of the JNA. When the Prosecutor asked Mr. Zaric why, on the 9th of May, he went to Belgrade, I wish to show what the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina was, because the 17th Tuzla Corps and the 2nd Military District, on the 9th of May, were under siege; they were blocked. And my next question to Mr. Zaric was going to be whether Mr. Zaric, or anyone from the 17th Tactical Group, had any possibility of going to the command of the 17th Corps in Tuzla, and whether there was a command of the 2nd Army District in Sarajevo any longer. And the only possibility open to them was to go and ask for help in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's -- I object -- I withdraw any objection on that basis, if that's the basis on which he asked the question, but that wasn't the way the question was put. If he's going to ask why did you go to Belgrade instead of somewhere else, sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, then. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, on the 9th of May, 1992, were you able to go either to the command of the 17th Corps in Tuzla or to the command of the 2nd Military District of the JNA in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no way. I assert that at that time all the barracks of the JNA in that area were under blockade of the Muslim-Croatian forces, or rather, the new Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was led by President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was this the reason for your going to Belgrade, to the security administration in the General Staff of the JNA in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of the reasons. The other reason was the very fact that we knew that these people had come from there, so we wanted to see at the very highest level who had sent those people there, and we wanted to let them know what these people were doing there. And if anyone could influence those people, and those paramilitary structures, we wanted them to do something, either to withdraw them or to stop them from doing what they were doing. Those were the two chief reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. Are you aware of the decision of the presidency of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the withdrawal of members of the JNA who were citizens of the FRY from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that decision. I don't know its exact date, but I do know that the order on the withdrawal of the JNA from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina said that all soldiers, officers, non-commissioned officers, and civilian employees of the JNA on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina who had been born on the territory of the FRY had to leave the area. I am aware of that decision, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You have already testified here that members of the JNA respected that order of the presidency of the FRY. Do you know whether all the members of the JNA were duty-bound to act according to the order issued by the presidency? And I'm referring to those who were on the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac and were part of the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the people in the 17th Tactical Group very well. Not a single member of the JNA who had been born on the territory of the FRY remained on the territory and in the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group, which later became the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, the volunteers, or the Specials, who arrived on the territory of the municipality of Samac, did they also withdraw to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This rule did not apply to them. They remained in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, did the presidency order apply to the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it applied to the volunteers, but in my view, at that moment, they did not have the status of members of the JNA, and the category of volunteers during a war is something I am not familiar with in legal terms, but I do know that this group of volunteers which arrived on the 11th of April, 1992, in Samac, stayed on this area after the 19th --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: As said by the witness.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, the Prosecutor put questions to you about the takeover of power in Bijeljina, Zvornik, and Bosanski Brod by Serbian Specials. I'm only interested in Bosanski Brod at present. Who took over power there, and when was this, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told the Prosecutor yesterday that in Brod, it was not Serbian Specials who took over, but in the night of the 25th and 26th of March, 1992, the regular units of the Croatian army and the HVO from the surrounding villages took power in the municipality of Bosanski Brod and perpetrated the notorious massacre in the village of Sijekovac against the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, I would now like to ask you -- I see you don't have your book, but I will hand you a copy. Could you please turn to page 259 and read only the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean after number 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after number 4. Precisely so. Just the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. "On the 9th of May, a date which we used to celebrate with pride as the day of victory over fascism, on orders from Commander Nikolic, I am travelling to Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have already testified that on the 9th of May you were in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's not contentious.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So you abide by your claim that on the 9th of May you were in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That is a fact which is a hundred per cent true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown Exhibit P140 ter. This is Mr. Zaric's interview. But all three interviews can be put in front of him, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, could you please find page 57. This is P140 ter, your interview of the 1st of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said page 57?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, page 57.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found page 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where it says "somewhere in early May"?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where you say that you were in Belgrade, on page 58, you say this was on the 9th of May. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And you said that to the Prosecutor during your interview. You mentioned this date.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is just what I told the Prosecutor in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This was your first interview, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My first interview with Ms. Nancy Paterson.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Would you please now look at your interview of the 3rd of June, 1998. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Would you please now look at page 56 of that interview.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I apologise, Mr. Zaric. Not 56, but 96. There's a typing error here.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found the page, 96, the page you're asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: It says here "Zaric," so it's your reply to the questions put by investigator Oleg.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Would you please read just a part of your reply as far as where it says "General Gligorevic, Colonel Maksimovic." So could you just read that part.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All right. "No, no, no, not that. But when I say this, it means that I can appear there. I don't know. I can testify here. I can see that. Colonel Maksimovic that I'm talking about is perhaps one of the people who know more about that, because he brought that document to the meetings so that we could see it. But Mr. Mikelic, it happened on the day when I went to inform about the crime in Crkvina, because the crime in Crkvina happened on the 8th of May, and on the 9th of May, 1992, I was already at the command of the security of Yugoslavia, and there were generals, General Vasiljevic was there, General Gligorijevic, and Colonel Maksimovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, you don't have to read any further. In this interview of the 3rd of June, 1998, you said that the crime in Crkvina happened on the 8th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You also confirmed that the very next day, that is, on the 9th, you had gone to the security command in Belgrade and reported about the incident; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And you stand by this statement, that the crime in Crkvina happened on the 8th of May, 1992, and that on the 9th of May you were in Belgrade, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You never -- no. As a matter of fact, do you remember if, in any one of the interviews, to any one of the investigators, you said that that crime had happened on a different date, on a date other than the 8th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not mention any other date to any other investigator, except that when I was talking with Ms. Nancy, we were talking, I wasn't specific. I said on the day in the early May when the crime happened, I went to Crkvina, but she didn't ask me specifically about the date then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like you to go back to your interview of the 2nd of April, 1998, which is 141 ter, and turn to page 58.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: There is an interpreted question of Ms. Nancy, where she tells you -- you're talking about the incident about the murder in Crkvina on the 7th of May. Do you see this? She asked you that question and you didn't answer that.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a question where Ms. Nancy put in the date, and she said this is an incident, the murder in the village of Crkvina on the 7th of May. And then she goes on: Do you know why people from the Territorial Defence went there?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In that interview, you answered Ms. Nancy's question on page 61. It begins: The incident in Crkvina. Look -- have a look at that answer and try to see if you confirmed anywhere in it that you confirmed to Ms. Nancy that the crime had happened on the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't find it in this part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I won't be needing these documents any more. Now I'd like to ask that the witness be shown P81 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, have a look at it and tell us - although I do not think that this is in dispute any longer - that the date when this decision was taken is the 29th of April, 1992, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor put it to you that you interviewed some persons in your capacity of the assistant chief for national security in the municipality of Bosanski Samac, so that my question to you is: When did you interview Mr. Sulejman Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was on the 20th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, you interviewed him before you were appointed chief for national security?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And when did Mr. Zaric interview brothers Bicic and Omer Nalic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was, to the best of my recollection, the next day after I went to Brcko, so it could have been the 27th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you conducted all those interviews with these persons before the decision to appoint you was taken?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't be needing this document any more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor put it to you that you were chief for national security and that in that capacity, in late May 1992, you went to Belgrade with Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, Stevan Todorovic, and Milos Bogdanovic. Now tell me: Before you left for Belgrade, was there a meeting of the Crisis Staff at which it was the decision to appoint you to the duty of the chief for national security was withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this meeting took place before we left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, the Prosecutor also put it to you that one of the reasons for the transfer of prisoners to Brcko was to get supplementary statements from them. Mr. Zaric, was there any reason which prevented you from possibly interviewing them in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'd now move on to questions which the Prosecutor asked you about the interview for Novi Sad television. Apart from Sulejman Tihic, Omer Nalic, Safet Hadzialijagic, Coner, and Izet Izetbegovic, did any other Muslim give an interview to the Novi Sad Television?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, Mr. Ramusovic, called Tota, a member of the 4th Detachment also gave an interview. He was wounded in that well-known incident which happened on the 2nd of April, 1992. And participants, not interviewees, but on the tape, there is also the recording of conversations with several citizens in Samac who gave their views about the state of affairs and how they saw those early days of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now tell me if you remember: To what ethnic group did these townsmen who were interviewed around the town were?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, of three females who were in that programme, two were Croats by ethnicity and one was a Muslim. I know that well because one of the Croat women was a woman who lent flat to me and my wife when we had got married. And the other two I know. Jasna Gibic, I know that she is a Muslim, and the other one, Ruzica, I don't know her last name, but I know -- that is, I think that she is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Were all the interviews aired in one programme, in a single programme of the Novi Sad Television?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tape that is used here as an exhibit is the tape -- the only tape that I saw. I didn't see anything else. So that all the interviews and the way that the journalist edited this tape, that is how it was aired, and all these interviews were shown at one and the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, were the interviews of Mr. Ramusovic and those females that you indicated used as propaganda against Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Out of the question. They told their human story on that occasion. It has nothing to do with this kind of propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Right. Let's leave propaganda and some other effects that the Novi Sad Television matter produced. The only thing I want to know is the following: In your interview to the journalist of the Novi Sad Television, did you tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. All that I said, it was based on the security intelligence information that I had collected until up to that time, the 29th, when I gave that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And the Prosecutor, towards the end, asked you a number of questions about your book, how it was written, what sources did you use, and you said that you had associates helping you with the book. Was that your answer, that you were helped by associates?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, will you explain: What did this help look like?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I write down what I think should be in the book and then these editors, language people, and other associates who helped me get this book published, they permitted themselves to describe certain things slightly differently than I had done, in a thesis, or rather, that I had sent them through my investigators. And that is, there are slight assessments, slight differences between what I intended to say and the way they intended to put it, in first person singular or in a slightly romance way, so that the book could carry a more powerful message of its author, in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And is that why there are certain imprecisions and inaccuracies in the book?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are a number of typos and a number of imprecisions, but I had no occasion to put it to them, because it was too late. I mean, I got it in the shape and form as you have it before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, where were you when your book came out?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was here in Scheveningen, in prison, that is, in detention, practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you now have a look at the cover of the book, that is, the back cover, and the Prosecutor put it to you that everything that the book says is true. When was that letter written, that is, this text which is printed on the last page of the book?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was written on the eve of my departure for The Hague, and it was only one of the interviews I gave to a journalist, and it was a kind of my confession in the form of an interview. And I wish to tell Your Honours that it happened that my departure for The Hague was made public in the Bosnia-Herzegovinian public, so that as I was about to leave, I gave many interviews to many people and I tried to explain there proudly why I was going, why I did not feel guilty, and that I believed truth and justice and the truth was the only way to justice, and I still believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, was this text written before, even before you started writing a book?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This text was written on the eve of my departure for The Hague. One of the journalists wrote it. They put my signature there, but I suppose that is some kind of iconography. I think it was the layout of people who were preparing the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before you sit down, Mr. Pisarevic, considering the discussion about the book, previously the Prosecution had asked for excerpts of the book to be admitted into evidence, if I remember. The excerpts that they were using. And the Trial Chamber was informed that actually the whole book had been officially translated, if I recall. The Trial Chamber is of the view that it's only better to have the whole book produced into evidence, so much reference has been made to it, and it's better that the whole, complete book is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by all means, but it wasn't my impression that a large number of pages of the book was tendered. However, Mr. Zaric's Defence deems that the book should be admitted as a whole, since fragments of it have been tendered and admitted, simply to avoid taking parts of the text out of their proper context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. Have you finished what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just wanted to find out whether any other Defence counsel wanted to say anything about this. I'll turn back to the Prosecution. Since the whole book has been officially translated and the excerpts that were admitted into evidence, the Trial Chamber would suggest that we use the same P number for the book, the Exhibit number for the book, and its translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: P181? P180? I formally tender Mr. Zaric's book, the English translation is "Crucified in The Hague," first edition, 1999. Five English copies and three photocopies of the original B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number, please. The Trial Chamber is of the view that the actual book in B/C/S should be presented to the registry so that the registry can have the actual copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The actual book, I think, is in the -- the Prosecution's copy is in its Evidence Unit. We can retrieve that or Mr. Pisarevic has his own copy there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. I think the Prosecutor should produce that, the original copy in B/C/S, the one which -- because it has the coloured pictures and --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Or maybe, Your Honour. If I may, maybe Mr. Zaric has his own copy, he put his signature and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's the copy which is published, the one which is on sale. The Prosecutor will make sure that the registry has an original copy. Yes. Can we have the numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, the extracts which were admitted on the 17th of April will maintain their exhibit number, P180 and P180 ter, and the full tendered book in English will be P180/A, and the B/C/S original copy will be treated as P180/A ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Bench has some questions to ask the accused, but before that is done, we are proposing that we have a break now and continue our proceedings at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Bench has some questions for Mr. Simo Zaric, and Judge Williams will begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Good morning, Mr. Zaric. I just have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zaric. I just have a few questions I'd like to put to you. The first question is whether the name of the paramilitary unit that Lugar was a member of, whether it was called the Grey Wolves. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour, the exact name of the unit. They never introduced themselves as an organisation that had a name. As far as I know, however, they did have an image of a grey wolf, an insignia of a grey wolf on their sleeves, on their armbands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Second, and related question, is whether you know or heard that this group, this unit, whether it was equipped or financed by the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't have this information. I know that at the outset, the police force in Samac did not receive remuneration for its work, in money, but only in kind. So I'm not sure I can give you a proper answer to that question, or a precise one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next question concerns your second trip to Belgrade, towards the end of May, 1992, along with Mr. Todorovic, Dr. Blagoje Simic, Mr. Miroslav Tadic, and Mr. Milos Bogdanovic. You mention in your interview, P140, that you met with a number of people, including one with the nickname of Frenki. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Frenki introduced himself as such, and he attended the meeting in the air force and anti-air defence building in Zemun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Was this man nicknamed Frenki, was his actual name Franko Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know now that this is the person, but at the time of the meeting, he only introduced himself by his nickname, Frenki. I had never seen him before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Did you find out at that meeting, or perhaps later, what his job was, what his position was in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I found out later was, as I heard, that he held a high post in the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, in the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear anything concerning his connection with the special operations unit, otherwise known as the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that, but my information comes from the newspapers. A lot has been written about this recently, and I found out in this way about his connection with the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And did the Red Berets have any role in the events which transpired in the municipality of Bosanski Samac in 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that this is the same team, but bearing in mind that the Specials sometimes did wear red berets on their heads, if we can make a logical connection between the two, then I might say that these people belonged to a part of that unit. But I can't be sure. It's a fact, however, that they did wear red berets on their heads. That was one of the uniforms they used during their stay on the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. My next question concerns whether, following the interviews that you carried out at the SUP in Bosanski Samac, whether you authorised or arranged for the release of any persons being detained there, including a Mr. Jusufovic and a Mr. Fadil Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no authority. But had I been able to, I would have done that every day. Neither did I talk to Mr. Jusufovic, nor to Mr. Sabanovic. I can only assume from what I know how Jusufovic was released. If you insist, I can clarify. But as far as I personally am concerned, I was not in a situation to release any detainee. I did not have such a possibility open to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether Mr. Zaric could have P127 ter put in front of him. Because, Mr. Zaric, I just have a couple of questions just for the sake of clarification of a few points in that. Fine. I'd like, if you could, for you to look at the second real paragraph, beginning with the words "first it is a fact that the Tactical Group number 17 command played a significant role in the war period, and even in the first days of the war." And then it goes on to say that this was concerning the organised arming of the Serbian people in particular. And my question to you is: In the pre-war period, and in the first days of the war, as this document says, how was Tactical Group 17 organising the arming of the Serbian people in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only way that arming was carried out through the 17th Tactical Group, and what I know for certain, is this was done through the detachments that were part of the 17th Tactical Group. The word "territorial detachments" is used here, but that is simply to say that these detachments were on the territory of the municipality of Samac and that they were represented by local people, people who had been born in the area. I do not know of any other way in which the 17th Tactical Group armed the Serbian people, except for organised detachments. At the time, as far as I can remember, there were five organised detachments of the JNA before the outbreak of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. If we could turn to the next page, the paragraph beginning with the words "fourth, when the war broke out." And it goes on to say: "First the Crisis Staff and then the War Presidency of Samac municipality came under the influence of a handful of individuals." I'd just like to know: Handful obviously implies more than one or two. I'd just like to have your, shall we say, impression as one of the drafters of this document, who that handful were, handful of individuals that privatised their positions in the civilian government, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, the Crisis Staff was a rather small body, in view of the difficult wartime circumstances. It did not have many members. When referring to the privatisation and some relations, I was really thinking of people like Stevan Todorovic, Simeun Simic, Bozo Ninkovic. These people who had the most influence, direct influence on many events in the area, and it's a fact that Mr. Blagoje Simic was at the head of the Crisis Staff. However, regardless of all this, I cannot ascribe to him these sort of intentions which I attribute to some individuals. In the area of Samac, Mr. Todorovic's, Simeun Simic's and Bozo Ninkovic's influence was very evident, and Milan Simic's influence. They had special connections with Mr. Crni and those Specials. That's why I put forward this assessment. I think they privatised their policy and turned it in a direction which the people of the area did not deserve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And if you could take a look at the paragraph on the next page, beginning with "seventh." It says: "Seventh, the War Presidency or executive committee," et cetera. And twice in that paragraph, it refers to the involvement of the civilian authorities in the military. In the fourth line, it says: "Influential individuals in the civilian authorities believed and acted accordingly that in return for all the material and financial assistance, they had the right to interfere most directly with the military authorities." And then further down in the same paragraph, it says: "The civilian authorities generally dominated the military authorities." And I would just like to hear your comments on that.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this unfortunate war, it was evident that the military did not have at its disposal enough materiel, especially enough food, cigarettes, and other basic needs that every soldier has when he is on the front line, or in the theatre of war. The army relied on the authorities in the municipality for assistance in this respect. I heard several times a sort of blackmailing policy. What will happen if we don't give you these things? And it's not only I who am saying this. When before the information was put together, I talked to people, I heard other people say this. That's why I thought there was blackmail of the military who were defending the territory. And I thought with reference to the second part of your question, that on the territory of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, five or six commanders were changed within a few months, and in my view, the reasons for this were that some powerful people in the authorities wanted to have obedient commanders, commanders they could influence. That is my conviction as to what was going on in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just one final question, Mr. Zaric. In the same paragraph, the last couple of sentences, beginning with the words "Family and ideological connections were also pronounced in the organs of civilian government, which formulated in a very perfidious way a political, material, and financial strategy, which was in fact a well-designed product and the implementation of private ambitions as the basic conditions for the bosses outside this area to get their share," and so on. It goes on a few words more. I'd just like to have your comment on those words, those sentences.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, there were attempts. I don't want to risk correcting something, but when several people bearing the same family name turn up in a government body, for example, in the Crisis Staff, there was Blagoje Simic, Simeun Simic, the president of the government was Milan Simic, one of the assemblymen was called David Simic. So these family relations seemed to be there, in my view, and that's why I made this assessment. As regards financial transactions, the people in charge, especially in the Executive Board, had power in disposing of material and financial resources in the municipality, and the bosses who are mentioned, the media also wrote about this, and it could not be concealed from us who were local inhabitants, that some members of the special units were given limousines, coffee shops, they were able to build houses, and that's why we thought attention should be drawn to this to prevent these narrow family and ideological connotations from emerging. That, Your Honour, is my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zaric. I have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: And the first ones relate to what happened yesterday, and I'm relying on my memory, because I haven't had access to a transcript from yesterday's proceedings. And the last questions I'm going to ask you are of a more general nature. Yesterday, during the cross-examination, the question of collecting away weapons after the takeover in April 1992 was brought up at least twice, once directly, and on the second time, more or less in passing. On the first occasion, you let us understand that the collecting of weapons, not only in order to consolidate the power of those who had taken over the town, but that it also was a wise measure in order to avoid an interethnic conflict. I think you even used the word "bloodshed." And even if you didn't say it, I understand that you meant the municipality of Bosanski Samac. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you. You didn't in that connection touch upon which the future consequences or implications would have -- would or could have been if such a conflict had broken out. Do you perhaps want to say some words about that, not to be too lengthy but in as few words as possible? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did not talk about this, but had there been a return conflict by some forces in town, if I understood you correctly, I think that the town of Samac would have been flooded with blood and the tragedy would have been far greater. That is my deep conviction. If you recall, when I replied to the Prosecutor about the collection of weapons by the members of the 4th Detachment, I said that this was only in the area close to the defence line, where we were holding positions, expecting an attack from Croatia, and the territory of Samac controlled by the HVO, and it was logical, or it seemed logical to me, that the soldiers on the first defence lines should not be threatened by someone in the houses behind who might shoot at them and who did not have the same opinion of the soldiers in the 4th Detachment that I had, and others who were on the defence line. There is no doubt that before the war, there really was division in the town, both along military and political lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I recall very clearly that you yesterday mentioned the imminent danger of warfare, and you let us understand that if the weapons hadn't been collected, the soldiers on the line would have run the risk of being shot from behind. And that means perhaps this is repetitive in a sense, but I think it's important to hear it also from you that that means that there was no strong solidarity between the different groups in your society, even if people had been living there for decades, not to speak about centuries. I think this is a proper and correct interpretation of what you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Your Honour, and that is precisely what our biggest tragedy is, Your Honour. Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: And I'll go over to a more general topic. Through your testimony, you have clearly denounced and condemned what happened after the takeover of power in Bosanski Samac, and it's not necessary to repeat all those sad things, all the atrocities and horrors that took place. It's well known to everybody in this room. But yesterday I think -- I think; I'm not sure, but I think I heard something of interest and importance. Perhaps I heard it only, so to speak, between the lines, or it might be that my memory doesn't serve me well. I'm not going to ask you directly: Did you say this or that? I'm going, so to say, around. And if you for a moment leave aside all the atrocities and all the horrors and bad things that took place after the takeover in April 1992, I put two questions to you which you can answer together or separately, just as you like. My first question is: What was, at the time when it happened, your opinion of the takeover of power in Bosanski Samac? And secondly, what do you, based on your long experience, think had happened if the Serbs had not taken over the power on the 17th of April, 1992, or in the days or weeks thereafter? These are the questions.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the first question, I have to say, and I have already said that, but let me answer you. I'm one of those people who were against any form of ethnic organisation of either municipalities or regions. So that would be my answer as to your first question. And the second question, had what happened in Samac not happened, that is, had there not been a takeover, then there is no doubt that Bosanski Samac would have come under the forces of the HVO, that is, the Muslim-Croat coalition, and Samac and Samac people would have suffered the same fate that the Serb people suffered in Odzak, Modrica, and neighbouring municipalities where the HVO forces prevailed. And there is no need for me to repeat how people fared in those areas which those forces had placed under their control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you so much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of some of the matters touched upon by the Judges, I would like to ask the parties if they want to clarify anything. Mr. Simo Zaric, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not know whether gentlemen from the Prosecution or the Defence have something, and I do not know whether that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Zaric. I'm asking the parties now, unless you want to say something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Anything from the Prosecution? Any matters for clarification?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zaric, in relation to the questions asked of you by members of the Trial Chamber, answer this briefly: Following the 19th of May, 1992, in the territory of the Samac municipality, at the 2nd Posavina Brigade of the army of Republika Srpska was active in the municipality of Samac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the commander of the brigade will be what rank [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the commander of the East Bosnian Corps who appoints brigade commanders, to my knowledge, as far as I know. And it is quite possible that such a person is appointed by the main staff, at the proposal of the commander of the East Bosnia Corps. I'm not quite sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the transcript, it's page 31, line 3. In fact, my question was -- maybe it's a matter of interpretation. My question was: Which authority is in charge for appointing the commander of brigade? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's now recorded and the answer seems to have answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And while this turns out to be an important topic, what can you do? I have to ask you that. Mr. Zaric, tell me, and I'm talking about the Samac municipality villages and hamlets in the municipality of Samac is there - how shall I put it - a sort of a grouping of last names in that region?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Specifically, are there the same last names in Samac, in the region of Samac, and at Pale, or in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a number of such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But we are talking about frequent last names, say, in the Sava River valley. Does it mean that we shall find the same type of last names on Romanija, or does it vary from one region to another?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And, for instance, there are hamlets in the territory of the Samac municipality which are even called after the most populous group of members of that community. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For instance, in the village of Pisari, the largest number, the most numerous, would be Pisarevici?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the village of Pisari, the largest number of locals would be called Pisarevici, in Crkvina, it would be some other last name, in Obudovac, you have a large number of people called Djukic. That is, for instance, what comes to my mind right now, but there are these phenomenon that you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On the Croat side, in the area of Odzak and in the Croat part of Posavina, you come very often across the last name Matanovic is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And of course, because of a very large number of Matanovic, many Matanovics we heard participated in the front structures for power, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, in the municipality of Odzak, several Matanovics held different offices during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But that, Mr. Zaric, need not mean that they are all closely related?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Simic is a last name -- no. Before that, let me ask you this: Shall we agree - and of course it is most difficult to talk about, because we are both laymen - but the most frequent last names among the Serbs are Petrovic and Jovanovic; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. If one really went into these ethnographic things, one might say that perhaps it could be that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And above the average share belongs also to Simic as a last name of these people?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, particularly in our municipality, because Simics do not all come from Kruskovo Polje. You can also find Simics in Batkusa and there are Simics who were inter-married and who therefore were not blood relations. But you could also find that last name Simic in other municipalities as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, I wouldn't repeat questions that I've already asked. We have the transcript and we shall have -- we can go back to that to see what was -- how Blagoje Simic treated Milan Simic with regard to appointments, et cetera, et cetera. But I'd like to ask you only the following: When, in the latter half of April 1992, the Crisis Staff was put in place, according to the information that you have, what was more important if one was to become a member of the Crisis Staff: To belong to different political parties, as we know, or to have the same last name? What was of more importance? Can you tell me that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's rather difficult for me to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But if you can, do then -- then please do. If you can't, then --

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps in the beginning, while people were still in a fluid state, then perhaps there were some people who in somebody's opinion were thought to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure how to answer this question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zaric. I have to interrupt you, because the question doesn't make sense at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And also, you should stick to the matters that were raised in the questions of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may -- I'm still, Your Honour, on the topic of family name, because that's surprisingly, but it seems that it's quite important for the Prosecution and also it's the issue which was raised by Her Honour Judge Williams, so I have to really comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since we are talking about last names, you will agree with me that the last name Tadic -- that Tadic is also a frequent last name in the municipality of Samac, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the municipality of Odzak, it is very characteristic, and the Tadic family is very large.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And my last question is as follows: On the basis of your personal knowledge, and bearing in mind the party membership of the members of the Crisis Staff in the latter half of April 1992, and you know that we're talking about liberals, reformists, non-party figures, SDS. What I'm trying to say is the following: Would you say that that body was, if I can put it that way, diverse in party terms, or were there familiar relations?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that their links were based on party membership. I'd rather say that the connection was similar political views, because one could be a liberal yet embrace the SDS policy or was a member of some party and then all of a sudden embrace the SDS policy. Then it doesn't matter. But to me it's important, what was one's political option and what one did as a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So if I'm getting your meaning, the familial relations were not predominant; is that so, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in those early days, no, they were not. That is how I would put it. But no, to be quite frank, and perhaps the word "familial" is too strong, because at that time I profoundly believed, because for the first time the discussion who was related to whom among the Simics was here in this courtroom. At the time when I was not aware of that fact and there are very many Simics on a particular body or on the highest ranking body in the municipality, it might be a logical conclusion, even if they were not related, I would have also liked to have more Zarics at my side, but unfortunately there weren't, and I was alone. Even if they weren't my close relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've finished with my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other counsel? Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. Could I, with leave, ask something in relation to that, arising from Mr. Pantelic's extended cross-examination which is connected to Your Honour's questioning of Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You wanted to put questions to Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, arising from what Your Honours put and Mr. Pantelic then extended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Very, very sparingly, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. I will do so. Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, your evidence was that you spent a considerable amount of time before you prepared this and drafted this document researching it, P127. It's the document I'm referring to. That was your evidence last week or the week before. I can't remember when at the moment.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want me to be accurate, I was engaged in preparing the material for about a month and a half. I don't know whether it is a long period of time. Well, if you wish, you can see it like that. But I spent about a month and a half after I arrived in the command of the Posavina 2nd Infantry Brigade to try to collect the basic information and to be able to write, to write my information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And when you prepared it, this is P127, the document we call the 13 signatories, and I'm only asking you in relation to the questions Mr. Pantelic and Judge Williams asked you, you carefully checked your information because it was important that it was accurate because it was an important document you were putting forward to the Posavina Brigade staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did my best to reflect in the information what I heard from the sources, that is, from the soldiers on the ground, and the way that soldiers and officers spoke about their perception of the situation, and then I talked with a group of people who were made responsible for putting it on paper. So I'm talking about the gathering information on the ground. This is not police work. It is the work of a morale man and something that should contribute, if I may put it that way, to creating a more favourable atmosphere for promoting morale in any army, and therefore in the army of Republika Srpska as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And when you referred to -- when you referred to family connections in this document, as Judge Williams asked you, you were only -- you were only referring to the extended Simic family, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have them in mind only. It just so happened that this subject was put on the agenda. To my mind, there were other familial connections in that rather narrow circle that I had in mind, of course, and where I -- and in places where I could hear something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The information you had was that these familial connections were enriching themselves, and that's why you put it in the document, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said how I came by that information, and the information that I came by was put in this information, and I stand by what is written in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that yes, the information was that these familial connections were enriching themselves, which is why you put it in? Is the short answer to that yes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if I mentioned the enrichment and those familial connections. I do not know if it was within that context. But bearing in mind different combinations that existed in the area, I also indicated such a possibility that perhaps these familial and family relations had something to do perhaps with somebody maybe acquiring better living conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And apart from the extended Simic family, what were these other families or familial connections that you are referring to who were within the small or the narrow confines of the civilian authorities, apart from the Simics, who were these other families?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to give names. Now you are making me think who was related to whom in the Crisis Staff. I know that Mr. Todorovic was related to some people in the S -- or some in the Main Board of the SDS, so that perhaps I could talk about such a combination. And about friendly ties between Savo Popovic and Milos Bogdanovic, now, these would be friendly ties. Simics, I've already said what in a way I thought. And Simic and another Simic, and I'm referring to Simeun Simic and Bozo Ninkovic, that is a kind of a party and friendship connection, because they have always belonged to the same type of political option. So that - how shall I put it - a heterogeneous mix of different combinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you said family and ideological connections. All I'm asking you is, apart from the Simics, and we know there was a large extended family Simic, even if the connections went back over some generations, what were the other families? You refer specifically to family. If not the Simic family, what other families are you referring to in the civilian authorities? Families. Please concentrate on family, as you've used the word in this document.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember it. It escapes me right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And finally, the living conditions or the improved living conditions you referred to, can you give us some examples of what you saw or what your research revealed about these improved living conditions, or the financial advantages which these families were gaining as a result of their position?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen, I didn't go to check the property and the financial status of individuals. These stories originated with men on the ground, and it was on the basis of that that we put it in. For instance, I know information which has never been investigated that 500.000 marks had been taken from the safe of the public auditing services, that this was broken into with special equipment, but none of the official bodies or agencies ever investigated that case. There was only the knowledge that that had happened. Where that money went to, well, had somebody done it, now I'd be able to give you qualified information. But as a morale man, I wasn't into investigation. I merely collected information as to what went on on the ground. Information, and if you follow the conclusion, we requested security authorities to investigate those cases, and so on and so forth. You listened authentically to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: As said.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to the witness Slavko Paleksic, who was one of the men who went there who carried out the control of the public security station and found an appalling situation there, and Todorovic told us here how everything was in line with the rules of service. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you for Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Simo Zaric. We have finished extracting evidence from you. You may go back to your seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I merely hope that you'd allow me to say something, but thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you can sit down. You still wanted -- you still wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. I will say something if you think it serves no purpose, then I'll go back to my place so as not to disrupt the protocol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. You are free. You can say what you want to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I merely wanted to say that last night I knew it was the last night which I would have before the last round of my testimony here, for which I had waited so long, and I took some notes down to remind me of what I wanted to tell the Chamber. It will take a few minutes because of my concentration. So if you allow me to share with you my last -- my latest thought, if it goes beyond the protocol that exists here, then of course I will not say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. The Trial Chamber can only allow you to say what you want to say, regarding the case against you, nothing outside that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's precisely what I meant to say, how I experienced this. Only a few sentences, a few minutes, if you will allow me. And when I start, if you think this is outside the case, please interrupt me and I will stop immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. What I can caution you about is that you have given your evidence in defence of your case, so you have to be very careful as to what you say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this mean you are allowing me to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I was just making sure that you understand that you've given your defence, and if you want to say anything, be very careful as to what you say so that it doesn't undermine your defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Your Honours, I belong, and I belonged, in the ranks of those forces in the area where I lived before and during the war, who opposed courageously, humanely, and unambiguously all occurrences and all those who advocated ideological, ethnic, and religious hatred. This had as a consequence a bloody civil war in which, unfortunately, war crimes occurred, as well as many other tragedies and inappropriate measures which were a result and product of the war. Had I not been what I was, from the viewpoint of the public post I held in the area, all I can say is that I was simply an unfortunate participant in that cursed war, like many others on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republika Srpska. I was a participant in this war who, within the limits of his physical and human possibilities, struggled to reduce the evil to the smallest amount possible, and I will never be able to understand what criteria I used to accuse someone of such a serious thing as a war crime, regardless of what segment is referred to, and thus be tried in the international palace of justice. There are many such innocent participants on the territory of the Republika Srpska besides me, and this means that I don't want to think that samples taken at random, or on purpose, have to bear the burden of all the victims and of all the countless people who behaved correctly during the war. It is very hard for me to bear the fact that the injustice against me has been so harsh that from the date of my voluntary surrender until today, I, along with some other individuals who are real murderers and criminals, those who raped, tortured, enjoyed persecuting and deporting people, that I am among them, among those who really deserve to bear the blame for the war crimes that happened. Freedom is the most precious thing a person can have, but it cannot replace the brutality against me which has deeply shaken me and my family and my people and all my sincere friends and acquaintances who know that I would never commit a crime, under any circumstances. I am aware of the fact that a conviction in this International Tribunal and a sentence awarded here is to serve as a preventive measure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you are going outside the perimeters of your defence, and I have to stop you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You may go back to your seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With regard to certain procedural issues, if I may address the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During the Prosecution case and more recently during the testimony of Mr. Zaric, and of course today, with regard to certain line of questions, the role of Frenki, person with nickname Frenki, Mr. Simatovic, allegedly head of special operation unit and recently indicted by the Office of the Prosecution, together with Mr. Stanisic, who was also head of state security in Serbia - we know that this indictment was issued, I believe, on 1st of May this year - and of course, Your Honour, I don't want to speculate whether the theory, Prosecution theory, would be to somehow to make any connections with Samac region and events in Samac. That, of course, is a matter for final submission of the Prosecution. But just as a step of cautious -- as a step of -- as a act of prevention, in legal terms, I believe that I'm speaking on behalf of all my colleagues, given the fact that from certain media we learned that Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic gave certain statements to the Office of the Prosecution, and therefore, certain parts of their statement might be of certain impact, whether it will be a Rule 68 or maybe we could paste them in the broad picture of Samac case. I don't know. I don't want to speculate. But the fact is that these two gentlemen, they gave the statements to the Office of the Prosecution. Actually, their investigators came to Belgrade, I don't know how many times, but the office of Prosecution is in possession of the statements of Mr. Franko Simatovic, aka Frenki, and Mr. Jovica Stanisic. So what I would like to respectfully move this Trial Chamber to order the Office of Prosecution to disclose only relevant parts. The Defence is not interested at all of, I would say, overall strategy, of the Office of Prosecution with regard to these two gentlemen, not at all. But in the interests of justice, we believe that certain portions of statements which are in possession of the Office of Prosecution related to Samac case might be, might be, of relevance for the Defence, whether, as I said, it will be according to Rule 68 or maybe -- who knows. Maybe there are some aggravating facts there. Namely, I'm speaking of alleged meeting in command, air force command, where Mr. Simatovic allegedly was. Maybe it's a logical way to conclude that since the office of Prosecution was in possession of this event, of knowledge of this particular event, maybe during the interrogation of Mr. Simatovic they asked him same question. So let's see and let's clarify this issue which might be of relevance for our case. So in conclusion, Your Honour, I would like to respectfully move this Trial Chamber to render proper decision which might be of importance for the Defence case. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. In view of the way you have put your submission, what you want is to ask the Prosecution to disclose to the Defence the statements you say they collected from these two, Simatovic and Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But specifically, the parts relating to Samac case and defendants here. So Defence is not interested at all of other aspects of these statements. So probably office of Prosecution can -- like, because they did that in previous phase of proceedings. They disclosed us part of the statements which are subject to disclosure, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Totality, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- specific about the two persons. I will ask the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic clearly knows far more about this matter than the Prosecution -- this Prosecution team does. Mr. Pantelic clearly knows that Bosanski Samac features in the Simatovic and Stanisic and Seselj and Milosevic indictments. This Prosecution team is unaware of the statements to which Mr. Pantelic refers or whether they are in fact statements or interviews, but we will certainly search and disclose anything that falls within Rule 68 or is relevant to the defence of the case, having now, on this day, been notified of the existence, according to Mr. Pantelic, of this material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just wanted to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour. Just for the record, the basis of my knowledge is certain articles from media and certain statements of Mr. Simatovic and Mr. Stanisic Defence counsel. So we learned recently that they were in contact with Office of the Prosecution, and therefore - maybe I'm speculating, I don't know - they know what they have in their hands. Maybe they know they have statements. If they don't, what can we do? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber is of the view that maybe by the next time we meet, on Monday, the Prosecution will be in a position to say whether or not they have anything. The Trial Chamber also wishes to note that most of these cases are related under the -- I hope that the parties should only be concerned with evidence which is relevant to the charges against the accused in this indictment. There's the matter the Trial Chamber would like to clear with the Defence, and this is regarding the question which was raised by the Prosecution motion regarding the deposition witnesses. This is whether or not the Defence would like to call any other deposition witnesses for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Defence for Dr. Simic does not wish to cross-examine any of Rule 71 witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Miroslav Tadic does not intend to call any of the witnesses for cross-examination of any Rule 71 witnesses, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Simo Zaric's Defence, we also do not wish to cross-examine any of the witnesses that gave their statement on depositions in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. We have the demographic expert coming on Monday, and after that we'll see whether or not we can ask each Defence to say whether or not they are formally closing their case. So we are adjourning our proceedings now. We'll meet on Monday, the 26th of May. The Court will rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of May 2003, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.47 a.m.,
